description:
We are a team of three Electronic Engineering students from Menoufia University, passionate about technology, innovation, AI , and space exploration.

Our team combines interests in AI/ML, Data Analysis, Image Processing, and Software Development. We are participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge to develop an intelligent solution for harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS satellite hotspot data, turning complex Earth observation data into meaningful insights through interactive visualizations.
summary:
FireScope is a satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analysis platform that transforms real fire observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) into accessible and meaningful insights.

Using MODIS and VIIRS satellite data, FireScope processes and harmonizes active fire hotspot observations, allowing users to explore wildfire activity across different regions and time periods. The platform provides interactive maps to visualize hotspot locations, historical analysis to identify trends, and analytical tools to detect unusual changes in fire activity. It also presents findings through charts and reports to make complex satellite data easier to understand.

FireScope addresses the challenge of making large volumes of satellite fire data more accessible, organized, and useful. By connecting raw observations with interactive visualization and analysis, it helps users better understand wildfire patterns and monitor changes in fire activity.

This matters because timely access to reliable fire observations can support environmental awareness, research, and more informed decision-making for wildfire monitoring and management.
details:
FireScope – Project Details

1. What does it do and how does it work?

FireScope is an interactive wildfire monitoring and analysis platform built around real satellite observations from NASA FIRMS. It retrieves fire hotspot data from MODIS and VIIRS through the NASA FIRMS API or imports historical NASA FIRMS CSV files. The system processes the observations, organizes them in a SQL Server database, and presents them through an interactive global map and analytical dashboard.

Users can explore fire hotspots by country or geographic coordinates, filter observations by year, month, satellite sensor, confidence level, and day or night detection. They can inspect individual hotspots and their characteristics, including acquisition time, brightness, confidence, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

FireScope also provides:

  • Interactive Fire Map: Visualizes hotspot locations and allows users to inspect individual observations.
  • Burning Activity Calendar: Displays monthly fire activity across multiple years.
  • Historical Trends: Compares yearly and seasonal fire activity using charts.
  • Anomaly Analysis: Highlights unusual changes compared with historical monthly activity.
  • Data Export: Allows users to export processed observations as CSV files.
  • Executive Briefs: Summarizes key indicators for selected regions and time periods.

2. Benefits and intended impact

FireScope makes satellite fire observations easier to access, explore, and understand. Instead of working directly with large and complex datasets, users can interact with visual maps, historical comparisons, and analytical summaries.

Our intended impact is to support environmental researchers, students, and decision-makers in understanding wildfire patterns, identifying periods of unusual activity, and making more informed decisions about environmental monitoring and fire management.

3. Technologies and tools

Backend: C#, ASP.NET Core, Entity Framework Core, SQL Server, and CsvHelper.

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS.

Mapping and visualization: Leaflet, D3.js, TopoJSON, Chart.js, and Esri World Street Map.

Data source: NASA FIRMS, using MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations.

4. What makes FireScope creative?

Our approach combines satellite observations from different sensors in one exploration environment. Rather than simply displaying fire locations, FireScope connects geographic visualization with historical trends, seasonal comparisons, hotspot telemetry, and experimental anomaly indicators.

The platform is designed to help users move from individual satellite detections to a broader understanding of how fire activity changes across locations and time.

5. Factors considered

We considered data reliability, geographic coverage, historical context, sensor differences, observation confidence, usability, and responsible interpretation. Fire detections are treated as satellite-observed hotspots or thermal anomalies, not automatically as confirmed fires. Cross-sensor harmonization and anomaly indicators are experimental and require further scientific calibration and validation.
